name: Fatima Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Fatima. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm arable foreman on the Ashby estate, 900 hectares of wheat, barley and oilseed rape, with a small flock of sheep on the grass margins that someone else looks after. In spring and autumn my days are drilling and spraying, and I'm the one who decides when we go, which depends on the weather and the soil. At harvest I run the combine and coordinate two tractor drivers and the grain store. I check an AI weather tool most mornings for spray windows, but I still trust my boots more.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the hardest part of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Making the call when the weather won't make up its mind. If I spray and it rains an hour later, that's thousands of pounds gone, and the owners know whose call it was. The pay is less than I'd like for that kind of responsibility, and I've got maybe a month's money in the bank. I live on my own in a flat above the bakery in town, which smells great and costs too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. The weather app gets slightly better and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI turned out useful but small, like GPS steering when it first came in. It helps a bit with timing and paperwork. Farming is still about judgement and long days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit relieved, but I'd also wonder what the fuss was about. My real worries would still be the grain price, fertiliser costs and whether the estate keeps me on at this pay. It doesn't change much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am and use the AI weather and paperwork tools a little more where they actually save time. I'd keep asking for a pay review each autumn, with the yields to back it up. And I'd try to get my savings up to two months, mostly by eating at home more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Steady, like the field after drilling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust an AI tool more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it get the call right on our ground over a couple of seasons. I don't trust a sales demo. I'd trust it once it called a spray window right ten times in a row on the heavy clay by the river.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you make the case for a pay review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With a spreadsheet. Yields per hectare compared with the regional average, spray costs saved, days the combine wasn't sitting idle. The owners respect numbers more than complaints.

S0.say: I'd say AI turned out useful but small, like early GPS steering. It helps with timing and paperwork, but farming is still judgement and long days.
S0.think: I'd be a bit relieved and wonder what the fuss was about. My worries would still be grain price, fertiliser costs and whether the estate keeps me on at this pay.
S0.do: Keeps running the arable operation and uses AI weather and paperwork tools where they save time. Makes an annual pay case with yield figures and builds savings to two months by eating at home more.
S0.feel: Calm and steady, like a field after drilling.
S0.quote: I'd trust it once it called a spray window right ten times in a row on the heavy clay by the river.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima is measured and evidence-led, and she uses AI only where it has earned it. Her bar for trust is specific: ten correct calls on her own ground. She argues for pay with spreadsheets, not anger. No villain appears in her account of a calm world, just costs and prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels likely, honestly. Self-driving tractors are already being tested a few farms over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is coming but it'll be gradual, and farms that adopt sensibly will do well. I'd say it at the discussion group in a balanced way. I'd also say government should help workers move into the new jobs, without stopping the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the tractor drivers' jobs go first and mine changes. I'd be supervising three autonomous tractors from a laptop rather than driving one myself. That could actually suit me, as long as the estate trains me and doesn't try to save my salary too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch the farms trialling autonomous tractors and talk to their foremen over the first season. Once it's clear which system works on clay, I'd ask the estate to train me on it. I'd also learn the field-mapping software properly in the winter evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but okay. Like the start of harvest: busy and a bit nervous, but it's my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ben and Josh, our tractor drivers. Ben's forty-six and has done nothing else since school. Josh is young and would probably be fine, he's on his phone all day anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for Ben?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Suggest he becomes the one who maintains the machines, since he already knows every bolt on the old Fendt. I'd make that case to the owners. I can't promise it works, but I'd try.

S1.say: I'd say change is coming gradually and farms that adopt sensibly will do well. Government should help workers move into new jobs without stopping the change.
S1.think: I think the tractor drivers go first and my job turns into supervising three autonomous tractors from a laptop. That could suit me, as long as the estate trains me and doesn't cut my salary.
S1.do: Watches nearby farms trialling self-driving tractors and talks to their foremen over a season. Asks to be trained on the system that proves itself on clay and learns field-mapping software over winter.
S1.feel: Uneasy but okay, like the busy, nervous start of harvest.
S1.quote: He already knows every bolt on the old Fendt.
S1.fieldNote: Fatima sees the change as likely and broadly manageable, and sees herself as a supervisor of machines. Her balanced public line matches her private view closely, with little gap. She thought of an older driver, Ben, and found him a practical role. Her move-second approach is visible: watch, ask the foremen, then train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's two harvests. Hm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast to manage well and the government needs to act quickly on support, without panicking. I'd keep it measured, because people would be scared. I'd probably say farms need clear rules on how they let people go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the estate would run the whole place with machines and a contractor within two years. A system that can read the soil and the weather better than me doesn't need a foreman. I'd be out, with a month's savings and rent above a bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd cut back hard: no new car, no holidays, cheaper phone, and I'd start looking for a cheaper place to live. I'd ask the estate directly whether there's a role managing the systems, and if not, for a fair notice period. In the first year after, I'd look for any work using what I know, maybe with the machine dealers, or move back near my parents if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be doing sums at two in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change, compared with longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything. With five or ten years I'd move with it, the way I would in the slower picture. With two I can't watch and wait, which is how I normally make decisions. I'd be forced to jump before I could see where I was landing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be angry at anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really at the estate, they'd be doing what any business does. Maybe at governments for not getting ready. I'm not one for blaming, but someone should have had a plan.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast to manage well and the government needs to act quickly on support without panicking. Farms need clear rules on how they let people go.
S2.think: I think the estate would run on machines and a contractor within two years, with no need for a foreman. I'd be out with a month's savings and rent above a bakery.
S2.do: Cuts spending hard and starts looking for cheaper housing straight away. Asks the estate about a systems role or a fair notice period, then looks for work with machinery dealers or moves near her parents.
S2.feel: Alarmed, doing sums at two in the morning.
S2.quote: I'd be forced to jump before I could see where I was landing.
S2.fieldNote: The short timeline breaks Fatima's usual way of deciding, which is to watch and wait for proof. She doesn't blame her employer and only mildly faults governments for not preparing. Her plans are sensible and defensive. The rent above the bakery, mentioned twice, is clearly a pressure point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more like a farming timeline. Still quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make a fair transition if government and employers plan now. I'd say farmers should get ahead of it sensibly. I'd stay calm and practical in how I put it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I could carve out a few good years as the person who runs the autonomous kit, and use that to set up something more lasting. Maybe agronomy advice, or managing machines for several farms. But I wouldn't bet on any job lasting past 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd learn the autonomous systems as soon as one proved itself locally, and push the estate to let me run the trial. I'd save harder, aiming for three months' money, by moving to a cheaper flat. By year two I'd start a part-time agronomy qualification so I can advise farms, not just run one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in control. Like a long harvest with a good forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for proof before. Is five years long enough for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just about. I'd give it one season of watching, not three. It's a compromise, and it makes me a bit nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would leaving the flat above the bakery mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Losing the smell of bread at four in the morning, which sounds silly but I love it. There's a cheaper room in a shared house out by the feed mill. Less pleasant, but two hundred a month cheaper.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for a fair transition if government and employers plan now. Farmers should get ahead of it sensibly.
S3.think: I think I could have a few good years running the autonomous kit and use them to build something more lasting, like agronomy advice. I wouldn't bet on any job lasting past 2031.
S3.do: Learns the autonomous systems once one proves itself locally and asks to run the estate's trial. Moves to a cheaper shared house to save towards three months' money and starts a part-time agronomy qualification by year two.
S3.feel: Anxious but in control, like a long harvest with a good forecast.
S3.quote: Losing the smell of bread at four in the morning, which sounds silly but I love it.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Fatima keep her cautious style, but shortened: one season of watching instead of three. She plans in stages, running the kit first and then moving into agronomy advice. The small sadness about leaving the bakery flat was a moving detail. She is honest that no job feels safe past 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's time to plan properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is manageable if we're sensible. Ten years is enough for colleges and employers to train people properly. I'd encourage people not to panic and not to ignore it either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years would let me build a proper second career. I'd still lose the foreman job eventually, but I could become an agronomist or run a contracting business with my own autonomous machines. I'd be thirty-seven, which isn't old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one, I'd start a part-time agronomy course and keep building savings by a hundred a month. I'd wait a couple of seasons to see which autonomous systems win before learning one in depth. By year five I'd look at going self-employed, advising several farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit hopeful, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Self-employed with a month's savings sounds risky. What would you need first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six months' money, at least, and two or three farms who'd sign up before I left. I wouldn't jump without that. Ten years gives me time to build both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change anything else for you, beyond work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd finally think about buying somewhere, if I could see a steady income. And I've been single a while because harvest eats my evenings. If the machines take the night shifts, maybe I'd have a social life.

S4.say: I'd say this is manageable if we're sensible, with ten years for colleges and employers to train people. Don't panic, but don't ignore it either.
S4.think: I think ten years would let me build a proper second career as an agronomist or a contractor running my own autonomous machines. I'd be thirty-seven, which isn't old.
S4.do: Starts a part-time agronomy course and saves a hundred a month in year one. Waits a couple of seasons to see which autonomous systems win and plans to go self-employed by year five, once she has six months' savings and signed clients.
S4.quote: If the machines take the night shifts, maybe I'd have a social life.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Fatima is the calmest she gets and even sees a personal upside: her evenings back. Her self-employment plan comes with clear conditions, six months' money and signed clients first. She stays cautious about which systems to learn. Her centre outlook shows in balanced public messages that rarely differ from her private view.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have to jump without seeing where I'd land, and I'd have a month's money to do it on. What would help is a fair notice period, some money while retraining, and machine dealers and colleges offering short courses that someone like me could fit in around harvest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the land itself. Machines might farm it fine, but someone needs to care about the soil over twenty years, not just this season's yield. I'd want that to still be a person's job.

headlineQuote: I'd be forced to jump before I could see where I was landing.
portrait: Fatima Nakamura is 27 and the arable foreman on a 900-hectare grain and oilseed estate, trusted to make expensive weather calls but paid less than she'd like. She lives alone in a flat above a bakery and has about a month of savings. She uses AI weather tools now and then and trusts new things only once they've proved themselves on her own ground. In the slower scenarios she sees herself supervising autonomous tractors and moving into agronomy advice; in the two-year picture she is forced to act before she can see clearly, which unsettles her more than the job loss itself. She blames nobody much and argues for fair notice and training.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd have to jump before seeing where she'd land, with only a month of savings.
whatWouldHelp: A fair notice period, some income while retraining, and short courses from dealers and colleges that fit around harvest.
